data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli settlers kill Palestinian grandmother in her home in Jericho
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Israeli settlers kill Palestinian grandmother in her home in Jericho
Israeli settlers shot dead an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded eight of her family members, including her children and grandchildren, during an attack on a home in the village of Ein al-Duyuk al-Tahta, west of Jericho in the occupied West Bank.
Eyewitnesses told Middle East Eye that armed settlers entered the Palestinian home in the middle of the night on Monday and shot 73-year-old Fidda Fheidat in the head, killing her on the spot.
The settlers, who had recently seized eight Palestinian homes in an area adjacent to the village, went on to fire at other members of the family, wounding eight of them.
Ahmad Fheidat, the victim’s brother-in-law, said that on hearing the gunfire, he rushed to repel the settlers.
He felt a sharp pain in his leg and realised he had been shot; looking behind him, he saw Fidda lying on the ground, bleeding from her head.
"Despite the injury, I rushed towards her and called out to her. When I placed my hand on her head, I saw that her skull had been split open by the close-range fire; her blood had splattered onto the walls of the house," he said.
Read more: Israeli settlers kill Palestinian grandmother in her home in Jericho

More than a year after signing a ceasefire deal, Israel is still committing genocide in Gaza and targeting Palestinian children there and in the occupied West Bank, a member of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory has told Middle East Eye.
“There is no ceasefire in Gaza. People talk about a ceasefire but at best it’s a reduced fire,” Chris Sidoti said in the latest episode of the Expert Witness Podcast. “The killing continues on a daily basis, including the killing of children.”
“The circumstances that gave rise to our finding of genocide are still operative inside Gaza. And until those circumstances change fundamentally, then the genocidal activities of the Israeli authorities will continue,” the lawyer and expert on international human rights law said.
Sidoti is a former Australian human rights commissioner who also served on the UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar.
His remarks follow two major reports by the UN's Palestine commission this year, including a report in June concluding that Israel had deliberately targeted children in Gaza, committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the coastal enclave, as well as further war crimes in the West Bank.
In October, the commission presented its fifth report to the UN General Assembly, finding again that Israel was committing genocidal acts in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
Both reports built on the commission’s finding in September 2025 that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UN migration agency warns of more Gaza hypothermia deaths, as Israel bars 100,000 tents from entering territory
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
UN migration agency warns of more Gaza hypothermia deaths, as Israel bars 100,000 tents from entering territory
The UN migration agency has warned of further deaths from hypothermia in Gaza as Israel continues to heavily restrict the entry of shelter aid into the territory.
Heavy rains swept through the war-torn enclave last week, inundating thousands of makeshift tents where the majority of Gaza's population is sheltering. A nine-month-old baby died from the cold amid the plummeting temperatures.
"Without proper shelter, without critical relief items, then hypothermia deaths will occur," Karl Baker, head of the International Organization for Migration's Gaza programme, said on Tuesday, adding that children were particularly vulnerable, since they lose body heat more quickly. "It's unacceptable to have hypothermia in the modern world."
Baker said that some 100,000 tents were prepositioned outside Gaza, but the Israeli authorities had barred the entry of items which they consider to be "dual use"- predominantly shelter items including tent poles and mobile homes.
Baker described meeting a drenched family sheltering beneath sagging, worn-out tarpaulins. "Gaza is turning into one large IDP camp (internally displaced persons). It ranks as one of the worst I've walked through," he said.
Reporting by Reuters

Saudi double-tap strike on factory in Yemen kills 14, Houthi health ministry says
A Saudi double-tap strike on a sponge factory near Hodeida in western Yemen killed 14 people and wounded 10, the Saba news agency reported, citing the Houthi-run health ministry.
Saudi aircraft struck the factory again as emergency workers carried out rescue operations and fought a fire, Saba said. Factory employees and emergency workers were among those killed or wounded.
In a separate attack, two people were killed and four wounded in Kitaf district in northern Saada province, the ministry said. Saba reported that the Saudi attack targeted a demining team and then residents who came to help.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran-backed Iraqi group refuses to withdraw from stronghold
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Iran-backed Iraqi group refuses to withdraw from stronghold
Kataeb Hezbollah, Iraq's Iran-backed paramilitary group, said it will not leave its stronghold despite the US-backed prime minister calling on the armed faction to withdraw and allow the army to enter.
On Monday, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi gave Kataeb Hezbollah an unspecified deadline to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakher, south of Baghdad, after the government earlier said an investigative committee had confirmed oil smuggling in the area - a claim the armed group denied.
"I can state decisively and with absolute certainty that the dream they dream of the Kataeb withdrawing from Jurf al-Sakher will not come true, not even over our dead bodies," Abu Taleb al-Saidi, a Kataeb Hezbollah commander, told AFP during a press visit to the area.
A security source told AFP that the deadline for Kataeb Hezbollah to withdraw from the area south of Baghdad was on Friday.
Saidi stressed that his group did not want a confrontation with Iraqi armed forces.

data.author: Maha Hussaini

Demonstrations gave Palestinians hope and pressured institutions to act. A ceasefire that has failed to stop the killing must not become a reason for silence
Demonstrators at the Red Line march in Amsterdam, Netherlands, on 8 November 2026, demand that the Dutch government take stronger action against Israel over its genocide in Gaza (Mouafak Mahmalji/Zuma Press Wire via Reuters)
Off
At 9pm every night during the first weeks of Israel's genocide in Gaza, around 30 people and their children in the home where I was displaced would gather in an empty space in front of the house.
Many of them wrapped themselves in woollen blankets, some sitting on the ground, others standing, looking for their daily "dose of hope" on a television screen.
With no electricity, we used the little power the available solar panels could collect from the sun all day to turn on the TV and watch the news for around 30 minutes.
Once the familiar news theme played, those gathering around the screen started calling on others inside the house to hurry and join them.
Among them, I stood, very well aware that those sparkling eyes would not find what they were looking for.
They would find no international action taken against the war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide we were witnessing, no appropriate international condemnation, and not even a statement by a world leader clearly naming the perpetrators.
Sitting on a concrete bench with an old displaced man from the shelter next to ours who came to watch the news with us, I whispered: "Do you still hope to see meaningful international action taken this time?"
He told me he was not watching the news in anticipation of any action by world governments, but found solace in seeing updates about the protests sweeping the streets of countries around the world.

data.author: MEE staff

Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/17/2026 - 18:29
New York City's mayor grew a moustache for men's health awareness. Some online critics saw something considerably more sinister
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani arrives for a press conference at Athens Square Park in New York City, on 17 November 2026 (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images/AFP)
Off
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has sparked a fresh wave of outrage over what may be his most controversial political statement yet: his moustache.
Facial hair took centre stage on Monday after Mamdani posted a video announcing the disbandment of the New York Police Department's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a controversial police unit responsible for both counterterrorism operations and policing protests.
But while Mamdani was busy explaining the overhaul, some online appeared far more concerned with what was happening directly above his upper lip.
For certain critics, the moustache was apparently all it took to transform New York City's first Muslim mayor into the deceased former Iraqi dictator, Saddam Hussein.
For a moment I thought I saw Saddam.
— Abhijit Chavda (@AbhijitChavda) November 16, 2026
Conservative commentator Will Chamberlain offered an even more elaborate interpretation of the mayor's facial hair.
"Trying to beat the allegations of being an Islamist by adopting the aesthetics of the secular Ba’athists," he wrote on X.
Apparently, the moustache had not only become a political statement but an ideological rebranding exercise, with Mamdani allegedly swapping Islamist imagery for the look associated with the secular Arab nationalist movement that once ruled Iraq under Hussein.
All this from a few millimetres of facial hair.
It looks like Saddam Hussein is running NYC.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/17/2026 - 20:00
Iraqi oil minister says Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline could reach capacity of 500,000 bpd with repairs and upgrades
An Iraqi government forces member walks next to a pipeline at the Bai Hassan Oil Field, west of the northern Iraqi city of Kirkuk, on 19 October 2017 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP)
Off
Iraq has resumed the pumping of crude oil for export through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan Pipeline to Turkey, as it looks to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Iraq plans to pump up to 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil through the 960km-long pipeline that runs from the Iraqi city to Turkey’s Mediterranean port, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said in a statement reported by the state-owned Iraqi News Agency on Tuesday.
He said the flow could reach 500,000 bpd after “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests” on the pipeline, which has been shuttered for more than a decade.
Iraq is one of the countries hardest hit by the US and Iran’s competing blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly all of Iraq’s oil exports exited the waterway before the US-Israeli war on Iran, and revenue from sales contributed to 90 percent of Iraq’s budget.
Restarting oil flows from Kirkuk to Ceyhan is the first step in Iraq’s efforts to reduce its dependence on Hormuz. Baghdad wants to connect Basra, its energy hub in southern Iraq, to the Mediterranean via the Syrian port of Baniyas and Turkey’s port of Ceyhan.
Middle East Eye was the first to report US efforts to revive a pipeline connection between Kirkuk and Baniyas. US ambassador to Iraq Tom Barrack hailed the reopening of the Kirkuk-Ceyhan line on Tuesday in a post on social media.
“Go Iraq, Go,” Barrack wrote.
